author: Kodao Productions
title: Church demands Pastor’s immediate release
content:
The police arrested a pastor of the United Church of Christ in the Philippines (UCCP) as he landed at Ninoy Aquino International Airport early Tuesday morning and is now detained in Calamba, Laguna.




Reverend Edwin Egar is undergoing arrest proceedings by the Criminal Investigation and Detection Group, UCCP said. Altermidya reported he is being accused of terrorism financing charges, a bailable offense.




The Church said its pastor is an active worker within the United Batangas Conference of its South Luzon Jurisdiction.




“His ministry has extended well beyond the confines of the church; he has been actively responsive to the calls and needs of the marginalized sectors in the region,” it said.




The Reverend was reportedly fresh from a missionary stint abroad.




The UCCP said Rev. Egar’s assistance to those suffering is not a crime but a living expression of faith. It called on authorities to ensure the reverend’s safety, respect his human rights and right to due process, and immediately clarify the legal basis for his arrest.




“Any deprivation of liberty or violation of an individual’s rights must be addressed with the utmost seriousness. The dignity, freedom, and rights of any person cannot be cast aside. As a Church and as people of faith, it is our duty to take a stand against injustice and to defend the oppressed,” UCCP added.

People in neighboring countries have not escaped the hazardous haze. Malaysia, Singapore and the Philippines have, in the past few months, raised public health and safety alert levels to try to mitigate the impacts.

hotspots

note

burned

Though the fires are the most intense in 11 years, 

burning

title: To protest is Constitutional
content:
“The 1987 Constitution does not require a permit to exercise the right to protest. This requirement was introduced by the martial law-era law, B.P. 880. However, B.P. 880 cannot override the 1987 Constitution, which guarantees this right. The right to protest exists because it is constitutionally guaranteed, not merely tolerated by the State.” —

content:

The city’s Bahay Pag-asa, however, refuses to release the remaining children in their custody, earning condemnation from the group Salinlahi Alliance for Children’s Concerns.




“Bahay Pag-asa [of] Muntinlupa must stop delaying their release and immediately, unconditionally, turn the children over to their families or legal guardians,” Salinlahi said.




Salinlahi revealed that Muntinlupa City’s Social Welfare and Development Office have instructed the children’s parents “to mislead paralegals” by claiming that the children must undergo another week of quarantine.




“If true, this is a deliberate obstruction of the children’s release and an additional form of harassment against already traumatized children and their families,” the group said.

title: Two Conferences, Two Distant Venues, One Unilateralist US Policy
content:
Nearly nine years ago, in November 2017, I faced criminal charges for joining a protest against the visit of then US President Donald Trump to the Philippines. He was in Manila for the 31st ASEAN Summit hosted by then President Rodrigo Duterte. What should have been an exercise of our constitutional right to protest ended in a violent police dispersal.




Water cannons, truncheons and even a sonic weapon were used against protesters trying to march toward the summit venues. I was among the progressive lawmakers and protest leaders charged with violating the Public Assembly Act, direct assault and disobedience to persons in authority. The police accused us of inciting protesters to breach barricades.




I considered the charges politically motivated, particularly since I was a sitting member of Congress exercising my right to dissent against a visiting foreign leader. The assault and disobedience charges were eventually dropped for lack of evidence that we had personally attacked police officers.




That experience exposed a familiar contradiction: government readily invokes democracy and national sovereignty in dealing with foreign powers but becomes intolerant when Filipinos exercise those same rights to question our relationship with a powerful ally.

title: Makabayan solon asks why Sandro’s district is getting biggest 2027 infra allocation
content:
ACT Teachers Representative and Deputy Minority Leader Antonio Tinio called on all fellow legislators who proposed infrastructure allocations in the proposed 2027 national budget to come forward and disclose their projects.




Tinio said that while the passed version of House Bill 10858 mostly arrange infrastructure projects under an agency, often DPWH’s Central Office or one of its 202 District Engineering Offices, proposals may be identified in the legislative districts where they would be built.




“This is precisely the information that the general public wants to know. ‘Anong mga proyekto ng congressman sa aming distrito?’ The public wants full transparency and accountability. Sa kasamaang palad, hindi ito binibigay ng House,” he said.




Tinio’s office reviewed 18,338 line items worth Php 641.3 billion under five categories: 1) DPWH District Engineering Offices, 2) DPWH Central Office, 3) Department of Agriculture farm-to-market roads, 4) DOH health facilities, and 5) NIA irrigation projects.




Of these, it placed 17,059 items, or 93.0 per cent, worth Php 541.7 billion, in specific districts.

author: Kodao Productions
title: Detained journalist Cumpio receives international award
content:
The International Women’s Media Foundation (IWMF) bestowed on journalist Frenchie Mae Cumpio the 2026 Wallis Annenberg Justice for Women Journalists Award in a ceremony in New York City on Tuesday.




IWMF said it honors Cumpio for reporting on social inequality in the Eastern Visayas region, including land rights abuses, the killings of farmers, disaster response, and the impacts of militarized conflict under government policies.




The prize was named after the prominent American philanthropist and heiress who championed various environmental and social advocacies such as the Liberty Canyon Wildlife Crossings LGBTQ+ and HIV/AIDS charities.




IWMF cited that as a student journalist at the University of the Philippines-Tacloban, Cumpio rose quickly within alternative media networks, becoming a leading voice in regional and grassroots reporting.




Charged with crimes widely regarded as fabricated, IWMF said Cumpio’s work – and her continued imprisonment – highlights the use of legal mechanisms, including anti-terror laws and red-tagging, to silence independent media in the Philippines.




The announcement of the 2026 Wallis Annenberg Justice for Women Journalists Award in New York City. (Photo by Vince Reasonda/Altermidya)

“We are saving so much already on gas and monthly electric consumption,” Badilles tells Dialogue Earth. Her family now saves PHP 20,000 (USD 315) each month for a system that cost them PHP 700,000 (around USD 11,000), she notes: “Even air conditioning [for the whole day] is not a problem anymore.”




Jovi Solomon, a café owner in Bataan province, installed a 40-kilowatt (KW) solar panel system to offset her business’s electricity costs, setting her back PHP 880,000. She says this allows her to save PHP 10,000 a month on her power bill.




Interest in solar power has surged as Filipinos grapple with skyrocketing electricity rates that have worsened since the Gulf conflict began in late February. However, the trend has also highlighted the stark gap between those who can afford solar options and those who are priced out.

When police from Davao arrested tabloid columnist Philip Lustre on Saturday, Oct. 24, 2026, right at the venue of the Saturday News Forum at Dapo Restaurant in Quezon City, serious questions were raised: That it was a Saturday and the cops should have given Lustre some slack on the pretext that weekend arrests are avoided to allow suspects the chance to post bail. Sad to say, this rule is not set in stone but written on murky water.




There used to be another deal between the National Press Club of the Philippines (NPC) and the government that arrests or investigations of journalists on libel, cyberlibel and other charges have to be formally relayed to the club to protect press freedom and the right of suspects to due process. Press freedom was upheld during martial law when imprisoned Satur Ocampo escaped from the clutches of a security detail when he voted during an NPC election. That exercise of press freedom happened during the incumbency of the late NPC president Tony Nieva.




Fair comment is fair comment and it is the task of the accuser to prove that there was malice in reporting, there was ill motive in the commentary and that some AC-DC operation was involved.
